title: What attention actually computes
description: How a transformer works out what the word 'it' refers to: queries, keys and values, the dot product, and why attention is a soft search that can be trained.

title: How LLMs watch video: beyond sampling frames
description: Why the default is one frame per second, and the ideas that go beyond frame sampling: tokens that span time, pruning what did not move, reading the video codec, timestamps, audio, streaming and agentic viewing.

title: Homeopathic learning: when clean data makes the poison stronger
description: A November 2026 paper (Clarke, Dubiński, Chua, Schrodi, Evans, Cloud) finds that poisoned fine-tuning data which does almost nothing alone can create a hidden backdoor once clean, contrasting data is mixed in. Covers the German-numbers, reward-hacking, bird-name and MNIST experiments, the blame-assignment explanation, and the limits.

title: Training without backprop: from 1.76 hours to 1.6 seconds
description: How the Noise speedrun made forward-only training of a small GPT about 4,000 times faster in ten days, from random activation nudges to Hadamard probes and identity-path credit, and what it does and doesn't say about scaling.

title: e-means: k-means in a tenth of the epochs
description: A deep dive into Meta FAIR's e-means paper: how mini-batch updates with exponential moving averages match 25 epochs of Lloyd's k-means in about two, what the evidence shows, and where the caveats are.

title: Expert weights as a compass: the P²-MOPD distillation paper
description: How learnable mixing coefficients on frozen expert task vectors make multi-teacher on-policy distillation faster and far more balanced, plus where the evidence is thin.

title: Robot by postcard: how a harness took Qwen from 2 to 31
description: A deep dive into uni-robot-agent, an open harness that lets a general AI model steer a robot through tool calls. Why the same open model went from 1.90 to 31.39 on RoboDojo, what the comparison with GPT-6 Astra really shows, and where the caveats are.

title: The avalanche that hit math, and why AI research is next
description: Two hosts walk through an essay arguing that AI research is about to be automated, the way math problems suddenly fell to AI, and why that could mean superintelligence by 2030.

title: The experts that aren't: what mixture-of-experts models really learn
description: MoE experts are not doctors in a hospital. A first-principles look at what routers and experts actually specialize in, from Mixtral's routing analysis to this year's interpretability work, and where the evidence is still contested.

title: The world model was fine, the planner was lost: 600 experiments on a JEPA world model
description: A deep dive into a 600-experiment study of the LeWM JEPA world model on Push-T: why perfect physics didn't help, why planning breaks past about 25 steps, and four training-free fixes (subgoals, a memory graph, symmetry, and ignoring the pusher). Based on public summaries of the write-up and the LeWM paper.

title: If pixels are too noisy to predict, why does diffusion work?
description: JEPA says don't predict pixels; diffusion models do it all day. Why both are right: 'noisy' means uncertain, and language models, diffusion and JEPA each escape the blur differently (list, sample, delete). Plus latent diffusion, REPA and pixel-space diffusion.

title: How NitroGen turns static into a button press
description: Why a game-playing model starts every decision from random noise: flow matching, the velocity field, and what each denoising step computes, read from the NitroGen source code. Script by Claude, voices by Gemini.

title: The Emperor's New Mind: can a machine see what's true?
description: A deep dive into Roger Penrose's 1989 book: his Gödel argument that understanding isn't computation, the objections to it, his bet on gravity and quantum collapse, and what the evidence says now. Made with AI: script by Claude, voices by Gemini.

title: Post-training for long answers: how one bit trains a two-thousand-token proof
description: How the weights change when the answer is thousands of tokens long: teacher forcing, replaying the model's own transcript with one advantage on every token, why shared tokens cancel across a group, and why long answers stall. Then the three fixes used for proofs: formal checking in Lean, cutting problems into lemmas, and learned forecasts, with AlphaProof, DeepSeek-Prover-V2 and Seed-Prover as examples. Replaces the previous post-training episode.

title: Cola2: plan in vectors, write in words
description: A deep dive on Cola2 (arXiv 2610.31305), a hierarchical language model that compresses text into continuous vectors, plans the next block with diffusion, then decodes words and re-encodes what it wrote. Covers the thermostat that sets chunk size, why smaller latents win, and why the headline of 43 times less data than Llama 3 needs an asterisk.

title: Training in four bits: how a model learns on a sixteen-value ruler
description: A deep dive into Thinking Machines' end-to-end 4-bit training of Inkling 2 Small: the FP4 number line, NVFP4 block scales, Four Over Six, why forward rounding noise is tolerable but backward bias is not, the transpose problem and stochastic re-rounding to 8 bits, Hadamard-rotated GPU traffic, and what it bought (about 2% efficiency for 8% faster pretraining and 20% faster RL). Compared with NVIDIA's all-NVFP4 recipe.

title: How to scale text-to-image models: the language-model playbook, applied to pictures
description: A deep dive into Wenhao Chai's handbook on scaling pixel-space text-to-image models on GPIC (100M permissively licensed pairs): why held-out loss beats FID as a ruler, iso-FLOP curves and about 50 image tokens per parameter, learning-rate cooldown instead of EMA, what FID misses about memorization, and why to drop classifier-free guidance. With background on JiT's clean-image prediction.

title: Back to the neurons: judging a neuron by what it adds
description: Two new Anthropic Fellows posts argue that single neurons are more interpretable than the field assumed, once you look at what each neuron adds rather than what makes it fire, and use them to detect harmful text, steer models and uncover hidden behaviors in finetunes. Made with AI: script by Claude, voices by Gemini.

title: Model Carving: which layers would you delete?
description: A deep dive on Model Carving (arXiv 2611.27962), where a Transformer deletes its own attention and MLP blocks during training. Covers the gate on every block, the pressure priced in training data, why the three headline numbers come from two different model families, and the appendix control showing the loss gain comes mostly from extra wiring.
